options.text: It's January 2022, and you're standing on the coast of Tonga, looking out at open ocean where a volcano is supposed to be. Underwater. Out of sight. Then the horizon changes. By the time it stops, according to the 2022 study by Wright and colleagues, the plume has punched more than fifty kilometres above your head. Not into the clouds. Through them. Through the weather. Into the stratosphere, and beyond it.

According to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, one eruption pushed about one hundred and forty-six teragrams of water into the stratosphere. A teragram is a million tonnes. That single eruption, they estimate, added roughly ten percent to all the water that layer already held, water now sitting above your head, between you and the ultraviolet light from the sun. A single volcano changed what the sky above you is made of.

Far from Tonga, a ground-based instrument logs a small, slow ripple passing through the air, the sort of wiggle nobody looks at twice. Then the same ripple appears somewhere else. And somewhere else again. According to Wright and colleagues, whose 2022 study paired satellite and ground-based observations from the surface up to the ionosphere, that one explosion sent atmospheric waves around the world, multiple times. No single source had ever been seen to do that.

Fifty kilometres is nothing on a road map. A short drive. An hour of your day. Now point that same distance straight up from where you're sitting. That is where the plume from Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai ended: more than fifty kilometres above the Earth, according to Wright and colleagues, writing in 2022. It climbed out of the troposphere, the layer that holds every storm you have ever seen, through the stratosphere, and into the mesosphere.

Wright and colleagues call the January 2022 eruption of Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai one of the most explosive volcanic events of the modern era. What they also report is stranger: atmospheric waves from that single source went around the world multiple times, a global-scale response of a magnitude nobody had recorded before. So why this volcano? Why did an eruption that began underwater produce a plume that reached more than fifty kilometres up? The answer starts below the sea surface.

why: It puts a half-watching viewer physically on the shoreline inside the first second and escalates vertically past the clouds, the weather and the stratosphere, and every claim in it, the January 2022 date, the submarine volcano and the plume exceeding fifty kilometres, comes straight from the Wright et al. study named in the line.
